```{r setup}
#| include: false

options(
  brms.backend = "cmdstanr",
  mc.cores     = 4
)
dir.create("fits", showWarnings = FALSE)

# Median and 95% interval of a vector of draws, as "m (lo to hi)", with an
# optional label inside the brackets and a typographic minus sign.
ci <- function(x, digits = 2, label = "") {
  q <- quantile(x, c(0.5, 0.025, 0.975))
  f <- gsub("-", "−", formatC(q, format = "f", digits = digits))
  sprintf("%s (%s%s to %s)", f[1], label, f[2], f[3])
}
pct <- function(x) {
  sprintf("%.0f", 100 * x)
}
```

# Linked zero inflation

This vignette provides code for fitting the linked zero-inflated model of @smith2012 in brms [@burkner2017] and Stan.
In the linked model, the probability of an excess zero, $\pi$, is a logistic function of the log of the mean of the count distribution, $\lambda$:
$$
\text{logit}(\pi_i) = \gamma_0 + \gamma_1 \log(\lambda_i),
$$
where $i$ indexes observations and $\gamma_0$ and $\gamma_1$ are parameters to be estimated.
Smith et al. [-@smith2012; -@smith2014] supplied R and OpenBUGS [@lunn2009] code for fitting this model, but OpenBUGS has now largely been superseded by more modern software.
In brms, the model requires only the zero-inflated negative binomial family that brms provides and a non-linear formula [@burkner2018], with no custom family or Stan code, and the functions for prediction and model checking (`posterior_epred()`, `posterior_predict()`, `loo()`, and `pp_check()`) work on the fitted model without modification.

Here is how to implement the linked model in brms, with `y` a count and `x1`, `x2`, and `group` standing for the predictors in any particular study:

```{r quick-start}
#| eval: false
library(brms)

fit <- brm(
  formula = bf(
    y ~ eta,
    nlf(zi ~ g0 + g1 * eta),
    eta ~ x1 + x2 + (1 | group),
    g0 ~ 1,
    g1 ~ 1,
    nl = TRUE
  ),
  data   = my_data,
  family = zero_inflated_negbinomial(),
  prior  = c(
    prior(normal(0, 2.5), nlpar = "eta"),
    prior(normal(0, 2.5), nlpar = "g0"),
    prior(normal(0, 2.5), nlpar = "g1")
  )
)
```

The linear predictor for $\log(\lambda)$ is declared as a non-linear parameter, `eta`, which then enters both the formula for the mean and the formula for `zi`, the brms name for $\pi$.
The zero-inflated negative binomial family in brms has a log link for the mean and a logit link for `zi`, so each formula is written on the scale of its linear predictor, and `zi ~ g0 + g1 * eta` is the linked model of @smith2012.
The two parameters of the link, `g0` and `g1`, are non-linear parameters, each with an intercept only.
A non-linear model in brms requires a proper prior on every non-linear parameter, so the coefficients of `eta`, `g0`, and `g1` each need one.
Because $\gamma_1$ multiplies $\log(\lambda)$, rescaling the counts shifts $\log(\lambda)$ by a constant, which changes $\gamma_0$ but not $\gamma_1$, so a prior for $\gamma_1$ does not depend on the units of the counts.

# Snapper in and around Te Whanganui-A-Hei (Hahei) Marine Reserve

The example uses counts of legal-sized snapper, *Chrysophrys auratus* (Sparidae), formerly *Pagrus auratus*, from baited underwater video deployments in and around Te Whanganui-A-Hei (Hahei) Marine Reserve, New Zealand, analysed by @smith2012 and, with two other reserves, by @smith2014.

```{r make-data}
library(brms)
library(tidyverse)
library(tidybayes)

snapper <- read_csv(
  "data/snapper-hahei.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  mutate(
    reserve = factor(reserve, levels = c("outside", "inside")),
    season  = factor(season, levels = c("spring", "autumn")),
    area    = factor(area),
    year    = factor(year)
  )

snapper
```

```{r make-data-summary}
#| echo: false
stopifnot(
  nrow(snapper) == 348,
  sum(snapper$count == 0) == 191,
  nlevels(snapper$area) == 6,
  nlevels(snapper$year) == 9
)
by_reserve <- snapper |>
  group_by(reserve) |>
  summarise(
    zero       = mean(count == 0),
    mean_count = mean(count)
  )
n_obs     <- nrow(snapper)
n_zero    <- sum(snapper$count == 0)
zero_all  <- mean(snapper$count == 0)
zero_out  <- by_reserve |> filter(reserve == "outside") |> pull(zero)
zero_in   <- by_reserve |> filter(reserve == "inside") |> pull(zero)
mean_out  <- by_reserve |> filter(reserve == "outside") |> pull(mean_count)
mean_in   <- by_reserve |> filter(reserve == "inside") |> pull(mean_count)
n_area_in <- snapper |> filter(reserve == "inside") |> distinct(area) |> nrow()
```

Each of the `r n_obs` counts is the maximum number of legal-sized snapper seen in any one frame of a video (MaxN), from `r nlevels(snapper$area)` areas (`r n_area_in` inside the reserve), `r nlevels(snapper$year)` years, and two seasons.
Zeros made up `r pct(zero_all)`% of the counts: `r pct(zero_out)`% of those outside the reserve, where the mean count was `r sprintf("%.2f", mean_out)`, and `r pct(zero_in)`% of those inside, where the mean count was `r sprintf("%.2f", mean_in)`.

Following @smith2012, the model for $\log(\lambda)$ included reserve status and season as fixed effects, and area and year as random effects.
We used Normal(0, 2.5) priors for the coefficients of `eta`, `g0`, and `g1`, which are weakly informative on the log scale of $\lambda$ and the logit scale of $\pi$, a half-Student-t prior with 3 degrees of freedom and scale 2.5 for the standard deviations of the random effects, and Gamma(0.01, 0.01), the brms default, for the shape parameter of the negative binomial.

```{r make-fit-linked}
f_linked <- bf(
  count ~ eta,
  nlf(zi ~ g0 + g1 * eta),
  eta ~ reserve + season + (1 | area) + (1 | year),
  g0 ~ 1,
  g1 ~ 1,
  nl = TRUE
)

pr_linked <- c(
  prior(normal(0, 2.5), nlpar = "eta"),
  prior(normal(0, 2.5), nlpar = "g0"),
  prior(normal(0, 2.5), nlpar = "g1"),
  prior(student_t(3, 0, 2.5), class = "sd", nlpar = "eta"),
  prior(gamma(0.01, 0.01), class = "shape")
)

fit_linked <- brm(
  formula = f_linked,
  data    = snapper,
  family  = zero_inflated_negbinomial(),
  prior   = pr_linked,
  chains  = 4,
  iter    = 3000,
  warmup  = 1000,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.99),
  seed    = 2012,
  file    = "fits/fit-linked"
)

summary(fit_linked)
```

```{r make-diagnostics}
#| echo: false
rhat_max <- max(rhat(fit_linked), na.rm = TRUE)
n_div    <- nuts_params(fit_linked) |>
  filter(Parameter == "divergent__") |>
  summarise(n = sum(Value)) |>
  pull(n)
stopifnot(rhat_max < 1.01)
```

Four chains of 2,000 post-warmup draws each were run with `adapt_delta = 0.99`.
The largest $\hat{R}$ was `r sprintf("%.3f", rhat_max)`, and `r ifelse(n_div == 0, "none", n_div)` of the `r format(ndraws(fit_linked), big.mark = ",")` post-warmup transitions were divergent.

The number of zeros in data simulated from the fitted model can be compared with the number observed:

```{r make-ppc-zeros}
zeros_linked <- snapper |>
  add_predicted_draws(fit_linked) |>
  group_by(.draw) |>
  summarise(zeros = sum(.prediction == 0))

zeros_linked |>
  median_qi(zeros)
```

The posterior predictive distribution of the number of zeros had a median of `r ci(zeros_linked$zeros, 0, "95% interval ")`, against `r n_zero` observed.

The function `add_epred_draws()` in [tidybayes](https://mjskay.github.io/tidybayes/) calls `posterior_epred()`, which returns the predicted mean count, $(1 - \pi)\lambda$, with $\pi$ computed through the link.
With `dpar = TRUE`, it also returns $\lambda$ (`mu`) and $\pi$ (`zi`).
Here it was evaluated for every sampled combination of area, year, and season:

```{r make-predictions}
pred_draws <- snapper |>
  distinct(area, reserve, year, season) |>
  add_epred_draws(fit_linked, dpar = TRUE) |>
  ungroup()
```

The predicted mean count for each area and season, averaged over the years in which that combination was sampled, is shown with the observed counts in @fig-data.

```{r fig-data}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for the figure"
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "Counts of legal-sized snapper (MaxN) from baited underwater video deployments in each of the six areas at Te Whanganui-A-Hei (Hahei), numbered in order along the coast, pooled over years, with spring and autumn side by side within each area. Areas inside the marine reserve are shaded pale yellow. Each small point is one deployment, jittered horizontally and slightly vertically so that tied counts remain visible. Each large point and vertical line is the posterior median and 95% credible interval of the mean count predicted by the linked model for that area and season, averaged over the years in which the combination was sampled. The vertical axis is on a square-root scale, which compresses large counts. Each predicted mean count therefore sits higher than the middle of the points."
# Average the predicted mean counts over years within each area and season,
# then summarise the draws.
pred_area_season <- pred_draws |>
  group_by(area, season, .draw) |>
  summarise(
    mean_count = mean(.epred),
    .groups    = "drop_last"
  ) |>
  median_qi(mean_count)

season_cols <- c(
  spring = "#009E73",
  autumn = "#D55E00"
)

# The areas inside the reserve (2 to 4) are shaded.
set.seed(1)
ggplot() +
  annotate(
    "rect",
    xmin = 1.5,
    xmax = 4.5,
    ymin = -Inf,
    ymax = Inf,
    fill = "#FFF5C2"
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = snapper,
    aes(
      x      = area,
      y      = sqrt(count),
      colour = season
    ),
    position = position_jitterdodge(
      jitter.width  = 0.2,
      jitter.height = 0.15,
      dodge.width   = 0.7
    ),
    alpha = 0.4,
    size  = 1.1
  ) +
  geom_pointrange(
    data = pred_area_season,
    aes(
      x     = area,
      y     = sqrt(mean_count),
      ymin  = sqrt(.lower),
      ymax  = sqrt(.upper),
      fill  = season,
      group = season
    ),
    position  = position_dodge(width = 0.7),
    shape     = 21,
    colour    = "black",
    size      = 0.6,
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = sqrt(c(0, 1, 5, 10, 20, 30)),
    labels = c(0, 1, 5, 10, 20, 30)
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = season_cols) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = season_cols) +
  labs(
    x      = "Area",
    y      = "Legal-sized snapper per deployment (MaxN)",
    colour = "Season",
    fill   = "Season"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

```{r check-fig-data}
#| echo: false
# The shaded band above assumes the reserve areas are 2, 3, and 4.
areas_in <- snapper |>
  filter(reserve == "inside") |>
  distinct(area) |>
  pull(area) |>
  as.character()
stopifnot(
  setequal(areas_in, c("2", "3", "4")),
  nrow(pred_area_season) == nlevels(snapper$area) * nlevels(snapper$season)
)
```

# Comparison with negative binomial and constant zero-inflation models

To check whether the link improved the model, we fitted two alternatives with the same predictors for $\lambda$ and the same priors: a negative binomial model with no zero inflation, and a zero-inflated negative binomial model with constant $\pi$.

```{r make-fit-alternatives}
pr_glm <- c(
  prior(normal(0, 2.5), class = "b"),
  prior(normal(0, 2.5), class = "Intercept"),
  prior(student_t(3, 0, 2.5), class = "sd"),
  prior(gamma(0.01, 0.01), class = "shape")
)

fit_nb <- brm(
  formula = count ~ reserve + season + (1 | area) + (1 | year),
  data    = snapper,
  family  = negbinomial(),
  prior   = pr_glm,
  chains  = 4,
  iter    = 3000,
  warmup  = 1000,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.99),
  seed    = 1,
  file    = "fits/fit-nb"
)

fit_constant <- brm(
  formula = bf(
    count ~ reserve + season + (1 | area) + (1 | year),
    zi ~ 1
  ),
  data    = snapper,
  family  = zero_inflated_negbinomial(),
  prior   = c(
    pr_glm,
    prior(normal(0, 2.5), class = "Intercept", dpar = "zi")
  ),
  chains  = 4,
  iter    = 3000,
  warmup  = 1000,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.99),
  seed    = 2,
  file    = "fits/fit-constant"
)
```

```{r make-loo}
#| cache: true
#| cache.extra: !expr tools::md5sum(c("fits/fit-linked.rds", "fits/fit-nb.rds", "fits/fit-constant.rds"))
loo_linked   <- loo(fit_linked, reloo = TRUE)
loo_constant <- loo(fit_constant, reloo = TRUE)
loo_nb       <- loo(fit_nb, reloo = TRUE)

loo_compare(loo_linked, loo_constant, loo_nb)
```

```{r make-loo-summary}
#| echo: false
cmp <- loo_compare(
  list(
    linked   = loo_linked,
    constant = loo_constant,
    nb       = loo_nb
  )
) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  rownames_to_column("row_name")
# Depending on the version of loo, the model names are the row names or a column.
if (!"model" %in% names(cmp)) {
  cmp <- cmp |> mutate(model = row_name)
}
d_constant  <- cmp |> filter(model == "constant") |> pull(elpd_diff) * -1
se_constant <- cmp |> filter(model == "constant") |> pull(se_diff)
d_nb        <- cmp |> filter(model == "nb") |> pull(elpd_diff) * -1
se_nb       <- cmp |> filter(model == "nb") |> pull(se_diff)

count_zeros <- function(fit) {
  snapper |>
    add_predicted_draws(fit) |>
    group_by(.draw) |>
    summarise(zeros = sum(.prediction == 0)) |>
    pull(zeros)
}
zeros_constant <- count_zeros(fit_constant)
zeros_nb       <- count_zeros(fit_nb)
pi_constant    <- fit_constant |>
  spread_draws(b_zi_Intercept) |>
  mutate(pi = plogis(b_zi_Intercept)) |>
  pull(pi)

# The text below states that the linked model ranked first, that each difference
# was less than twice its standard error, and that both alternatives predicted
# fewer zeros than were observed.
stopifnot(
  cmp$model[1] == "linked",
  d_constant > 0,
  d_nb > 0,
  d_constant < 2 * se_constant,
  d_nb < 2 * se_nb,
  median(zeros_constant) < n_zero,
  median(zeros_nb) < n_zero
)
```

Expected log predictive density, estimated by Pareto-smoothed importance-sampling leave-one-out cross-validation [PSIS-LOO, @vehtari2017], was greatest for the linked model, exceeding that of the model with constant $\pi$ by `r sprintf("%.1f", d_constant)` (SE `r sprintf("%.1f", se_constant)`) and that of the negative binomial model by `r sprintf("%.1f", d_nb)` (SE `r sprintf("%.1f", se_nb)`).
Each difference was less than twice its standard error, so the support for the link from these data is moderate.
Observations with a Pareto $k$ value above 0.7, the threshold above which PSIS-LOO estimates are unreliable [@vehtari2017], were handled by refitting the model without them (`reloo = TRUE`).

The model with constant $\pi$ estimated a probability of an excess zero of `r ci(pi_constant)`.
The median number of zeros predicted was `r round(median(zeros_constant))` for the model with constant $\pi$ and `r round(median(zeros_nb))` for the negative binomial model, against `r n_zero` observed and `r round(median(zeros_linked$zeros))` for the linked model.
A constant $\pi$ applies equally to deployments inside and outside the reserve, whereas the proportion of zeros was `r pct(zero_out)`% outside and `r pct(zero_in)`% inside.

# Estimated relationship between zero inflation and the mean count

```{r make-link-estimates}
fit_linked |>
  gather_draws(b_g0_Intercept, b_g1_Intercept) |>
  median_qi()
```

```{r make-link-summary}
#| echo: false
link_draws <- fit_linked |>
  spread_draws(b_g0_Intercept, b_g1_Intercept)
g0 <- link_draws$b_g0_Intercept
g1 <- link_draws$b_g1_Intercept

pi_by_reserve <- pred_draws |>
  group_by(.draw, reserve) |>
  summarise(
    pi      = mean(zi),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
pi_out <- pi_by_reserve |> filter(reserve == "outside") |> pull(pi)
pi_in  <- pi_by_reserve |> filter(reserve == "inside") |> pull(pi)
n_cells <- pred_draws |> distinct(area, year, season) |> nrow()
stopifnot(median(g1) < 0)
```

The probability of an excess zero decreased as the mean count increased, with a posterior median for $\gamma_1$ of `r ci(g1, 2, "95% credible interval ")`, and for $\gamma_0$ of `r ci(g0)` (@fig-link).
Averaged over the `r n_cells` sampled combinations of area, year, and season, the probability of an excess zero was `r ci(pi_out)` outside the reserve and `r ci(pi_in)` inside.

```{r fig-link}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for the figure"
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "Estimated relationship between the probability of an excess zero, $\\pi$, and the mean of the negative binomial component, $\\lambda$, for legal-sized snapper at Hahei, under the linked model $\\text{logit}(\\pi) = \\gamma_0 + \\gamma_1 \\log(\\lambda)$. The black line is the posterior median of $\\pi$ at each value of $\\lambda$, and the grey lines are the relationship for 100 draws from the posterior distribution of $\\gamma_0$ and $\\gamma_1$. Each point marks the posterior medians of $\\lambda$ and $\\pi$ for one sampled combination of area, year, and season, coloured by reserve status. The horizontal axis is on a log scale."
# The relationship for every posterior draw, over a grid of lambda.
curves <- link_draws |>
  expand_grid(lambda = exp(seq(log(0.1), log(20), length.out = 100))) |>
  mutate(pi = plogis(b_g0_Intercept + b_g1_Intercept * log(lambda)))

median_curve <- curves |>
  group_by(lambda) |>
  summarise(pi = median(pi))

set.seed(2012)
curves_100 <- curves |>
  filter(.draw %in% sample(unique(.draw), 100))

# Posterior medians of lambda and pi for each sampled combination.
cell_points <- pred_draws |>
  group_by(area, reserve, year, season) |>
  summarise(
    lambda  = median(mu),
    pi      = median(zi),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot() +
  geom_line(
    data = curves_100,
    aes(
      x     = lambda,
      y     = pi,
      group = .draw
    ),
    colour    = "grey60",
    alpha     = 0.3,
    linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = median_curve,
    aes(
      x = lambda,
      y = pi
    ),
    linewidth = 0.9
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = cell_points,
    aes(
      x      = lambda,
      y      = pi,
      colour = reserve
    ),
    size = 1.5
  ) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(
      outside = "#D55E00",
      inside  = "#0072B2"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    x      = expression("Mean of the negative binomial component (" * lambda * ")"),
    y      = expression("Probability of an excess zero (" * pi * ")"),
    colour = "Reserve status"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

# Reserve effect

The reserve effect is the ratio of the mean count inside the reserve to the mean count outside it, computed within each posterior draw from the predicted mean counts in `pred_draws`:

```{r make-reserve-effect}
reserve_effect <- pred_draws |>
  group_by(.draw, reserve) |>
  summarise(
    mean_count = mean(.epred),
    .groups    = "drop"
  ) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from  = reserve,
    values_from = mean_count
  ) |>
  mutate(ratio = inside / outside)

reserve_effect |>
  median_qi(ratio)
```

```{r check-reserve-effect}
#| echo: false
# posterior_epred() should equal (1 - pi) * lambda for every cell and draw.
max_rel_diff <- pred_draws |>
  summarise(d = max(abs(.epred - (1 - zi) * mu) / .epred)) |>
  pull(d)
stopifnot(max_rel_diff < 1e-8)
# The text below states that this estimate is smaller than the published 16.36.
stopifnot(median(reserve_effect$ratio) < 0.8 * 16.36)
```

Averaged over the `r n_cells` sampled combinations of area, year, and season, with equal weight for each, mean counts were `r ci(reserve_effect$ratio, 1)` times greater inside the reserve than outside.
This ratio applies to the areas and years that were sampled, and does not include the variation expected among new areas or years.
The ratio is smaller than the 16.4 reported by @smith2012, which evaluated $(1 - \pi)\lambda$ at zero area, year, and season effects instead of averaging it over them.

# Other implementations

@anderson2022 fitted the zero-inflated negative binomial with the link of @smith2012, which they called ZINBL, by maximum likelihood in the R package [senlm](https://primer-e.github.io/senlm/), with a non-linear function for the mean response of a species along a single environmental gradient.
@rabel2023 fitted a Bayesian version in Stan, also along a single gradient, in the R package [modskurt](https://hdrab127.github.io/modskurt/) ([source on GitHub](https://github.com/hdrab127/modskurt)), with $\pi$ linked to the mean count divided by the peak mean count along the gradient, rather than to the log of the mean count.
